title: How to Convince Investors: Convince yourself first, then tell the truth
summary: Graham argues founders should stop relying on pitch skills and instead make a startup worth investing in, understand why, and explain it plainly. Investors want formidable founders and a plausible path to owning a big piece of a big market. Seeming formidable comes from truth and domain expertise, not swagger.

principles.text: Don't pitch with your back. Understand why your startup is worth investing in, then simply explain it well.
principles.quote: Most would be better off if they let their startup do the work — if they started by understanding why their startup is worth investing in, then simply explained this well to investors.

principles.text: Investors decide fast whether you're a winner, and that first impression colors how they read everything else about your startup.
principles.quote: If investors are impressed with you as founders, they say they want to invest because it's a rich market, and if not, they say they can't invest because of the slow sales cycle.

principles.text: Inexperienced founders seem most formidable by sticking to the truth, not by imitating swagger.
principles.quote: Investors are not always that good at judging technology, but they're good at judging confidence. If you try to act like something you're not, you'll just end up in an uncanny valley.

principles.text: Truly evaluate whether your startup is worth investing in; if it isn't, don't raise. You need domain expertise to judge this.
principles.quote: I mean truly evaluate whether your startup is worth investing in. If it isn't, don't try to raise money.

principles.text: Raise when you can convince investors, not when you need money or hit an artificial deadline.
principles.quote: The time to raise money is not when you need it, or when you reach some artificial deadline like a Demo Day. It's when you can convince investors, and not before.

principles.text: Investors think in markets, not ideas. You need a plausible path to owning a big piece of a big market, riding a 'why now' wave.
principles.quote: Founders think of startups as ideas, but investors think of them as markets.
